title: The bed of arrows
hook: two kinds of arrows reach Bhishma, and he can tell them apart
carry: uttarayana: even the hour of death is sacred
tomorrow: his head is hanging down. what pillow will he take?

segments.voice: Yesterday we went back a lifetime, to Amba, born again as Shikhandi. Your line: karma can follow you into another birth.

Two kinds of arrows are flying at Bhishma's chariot. Some come from Shikhandi, standing in front, exactly as Bhishma himself advised. Bhishma doesn't answer them. He keeps his bow lowered toward that one warrior, the way he said he would. And behind Shikhandi, using him as cover, Arjuna is shooting too. Bhishma has trained and fought beside these archers for a lifetime. Today, the moment he stops guessing whose arrows are reaching him.

In Ganguli's English, Bhishma speaks as the arrows pierce him. These aren't Shikhandi's, he says, in effect. They cut too deep. These are Arjuna's. Still he doesn't turn his weapons on Shikhandi. Then he falls from his chariot. So many arrows are lodged in him that he never touches the ground. He lies on them, held above the earth, on a bed of arrows. The fighting stops. Both sides gather around the same old man. And Bhishma doesn't die. Long ago his father gave him a gift for his vow: he would die only when he chose. Hindus call it ichchha-mrityu, death at will. Lying there, he sees the sun in its southern course and decides it isn't yet time. Sages come to him as swans, sent by his mother, the river goddess Ganga, and he tells them he'll hold on until the sun turns north. Here's why that matters. Hindu tradition treats the sun's northern half of the year, uttarayana, as the bright, auspicious time, and the Bhagavad Gita names those six months among the bright paths by which those who know God depart. So Bhishma doesn't just pick a day. He picks a holy one. Hindus still keep the memory: Makar Sankranti is celebrated as the sun's turn north, and Bhishma Ashtami, a few weeks later, marks the day tradition says he let go. The teaching: in Hinduism, the hour of leaving this life isn't something to hide from. It can be faced, prepared for, and offered to God.
screen: `THESE ARE ARJUNA'S ARROWS` · `DEATH AT WILL` · `WAITING FOR THE SUN` · then, large: `UTTARAYANA`

segments.voice: Turn toward wherever the sun is right now, even through a wall. Many Hindus greet the sun each morning, palms together or pouring out a little water, with a simple line: Om suryaya namah. I bow to the sun. Breathe in and feel the light on your face, or imagine it. Breathe out and say the line once, silently or aloud. If you pray, let the greeting be your prayer. If you don't, let the light remind you that your days have a direction.
Bhishma's fall. The grandsire on a bed of arrows, held above the ground, waiting for the sun to turn north.
Your line: uttarayana: even the hour of death is sacred. Bhishma chose a holy one. Day eight hundred twenty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindus remember Bhishma around Makar Sankranti and on Bhishma Ashtami, and the bed of arrows, in Sanskrit shara-shayya, appears in temple art, paintings and retellings of the epic.

fork.setup: your cousin says the Hindu idea of a good time to die is just superstition. by Bhishma's story, what's closest?
options: given the choice, Bhishma waited for uttarayana, the holy northern course of the sun; the hour of leaving can be offered to God.
Bhishma only waited because he was too stubborn to give up.
timing mattered only for kings and warriors, never for ordinary people.
fork.reveal: Bhishma could die whenever he chose, and he chose the sun's bright, northern half, the time the Gita names among the bright paths.

original.note: bed of arrows: the name for Bhishma's resting place on the field.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bhishma was killed in battle.
what it means: he was brought down, but by his father's gift he chose when he would die.

what a scholar hears: the Gita names the sun's northern course among the bright paths of departure, so Bhishma's waiting is devotion as well as endurance, and the battlefield becomes a deathbed where he will teach.

chat.says: Nani was telling Sam about Sankranti and said even Bhishma waited for it before he died. Sam: 'why would anyone WAIT to die??' wait, why?
options: uttarayana, the sun's northern half, is a holy time; Bhishma could choose his hour, so he chose a sacred one.

chat.meaning: Bhishma could die only when he chose. On the bed of arrows he waited for the sun to turn north, uttarayana, which Hindus hold to be a holy time.
